description: When I was working on the video for yesterday's song, I wanted to make it look like the character in the video kept turning their face and their body to look at a different camera. It didn't work at all; I am terrible with spatial reasoning. But I had written out a guide for myself, of what I thought the right progression was. It was not the right progression, but then today when I sat down to do my song, i realized the guide I had written looked like lyrics. So I sang them. title: My Heart Is Still In Westford
description: So there's this guy named David Kahn Feurzeig who is a composition professor at the University of Vermont. He's doing a thing called "Every Town Vermont" where he plays a show in every single town in Vermont. In each town, he tailors the performance in someway, for instance, playing a piece from the year the town was founded. Well, for my tiny hometown of Westford, he composed a song in my honor! I guess he searched Wikipedia, and I came up as a "notable person" from there. Anyway, I watched a video of him performing his delightful homage (he wrote the song in a day), and it made me miss Vermont and Westford so much that I decided to write this song in response.

title: Crypto Tax Nightmare
description:
The story behind this song ended in March 2024, when I sold my Autoglyph and used the $1.1 million proceeds to pay my tax bill. The day after I paid, I began writing this song. I've worked on it on and off for the past year and a half.
Originally, this wasn't going to be Song #6000, but as the song and video evolved, I started to feel the message was one I wanted to amplify with the hoopla of this milestone.
Something not everyone will notice: Almost every scene references a music video from the 80s or 90s. I’d love for someone in the comments to see if they can call out every single one with a timestamp. Each reference has personal meaning—these are the videos I watched from childhood through my teenage years. They all contributed, in one way or another, to my dream of becoming a musician.
Why use them? As a young teenager, I believed that getting a music video on MTV was how you knew you'd "made it."
Fast forward to 2022, when I made $3 million. For a moment, I felt like I had "made it." But even before the tax nightmare began, I remember thinking, "Now what?"
The music video—and specifically its near-obsolescence as a medium (especially as an MTV-based medium)—serves as a reminder that there's no such thing as "making it." Rather, I am "making it" every single day I sit down to write my song.
I hope you enjoy the story!
